meta.blurb: Arsène Lupin robs the rich, outwits the police and always keeps his word. Nine daring adventures take him from a stormy ocean liner to a prison cell, a castle with a secret passage, and a meeting with Sherlock Holmes.
meta.bible: Arsène Lupin: the gentleman-burglar, a master of disguises, charming, daring and fond of a joke; he also appears as Bernard d'Andrézy, Guillaume Berlat, Jean Daspry, Horace Velmont and Grimaudan. Inspector Ganimard: the old, patient detective who arrests Lupin and never quite catches him. Monsieur Dudouis: Chief of the Sûreté. The Arrest of Arsène Lupin: La Provence, a liner crossing to New York. Miss Nelly Underdown: a rich, kind young woman. Lady Jerland: her friend. Monsieur Rozaine: a pale, fair-haired passenger. Major Rawson. Arsène Lupin in Prison: Baron Nathan Cahorn lives alone in the Château de Malaquis, a castle on a rock in the Seine, with his Rubens and Watteau paintings. Caudebec: the nearby town. Prison de la Santé: the Paris prison. The Escape of Arsène Lupin: Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant. Judge Jules Bouvier. Désiré Baudru: a poor man who looks a little like Lupin. Bois de Boulogne: the park in Paris. The Mysterious Traveller: Madame Renaud, a nervous lady; Rouen; Pierre Onfrey, a wanted criminal; the policemen Massol and Delivet; Darnétal. The Queen's Necklace: the Count and Countess de Dreux-Soubise; Henriette, a poor friend of the countess; her small son Raoul; the Chevalier Floriani. The Seven of Hearts: Jean Daspry; Georges Andermatt, a banker, and Madame Andermatt; the brothers Etienne and Alfred Varin; the engineer Louis Lacombe; Salvator, a mystery writer in the newspaper Echo de France; Neuilly. Madame Imbert's Safe: Ludovic Imbert and Gervaise Imbert; André Brawford. The Black Pearl: the Countess d'Andillot, once the singer Léotine Zalti; Victor Danègre, her servant; Mademoiselle de Sinclèves; avenue Hoche; Parc Monceau; Montmartre. Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late: the Château de Thibermesnil near Dieppe; the banker Georges Devanne; Father Gélis; Sherlock Holmes, the English detective; Duke Rollo; Sully; King Louis the Sixteenth; Hall of the Guards; Tour Guillaume. Paris. France. America. New York. Chicago. England. Voice and tone: light, quick and witty, full of cunning plans and elegant jokes; thefts are never violent, and every deed ends with a surprise.

beats.scene: An ocean liner crosses a stormy sea at night
beats.summary: In The Arrest of Arsène Lupin, a wireless message tells the passengers of La Provence that the thief Arsène Lupin is on board.

beats.scene: Passengers on a deck study a list of names beside a pale young man
beats.summary: Miss Nelly Underdown and Bernard d'Andrézy find from the passenger list that the only suspect is Monsieur Rozaine, fair-haired, alone, with a name beginning with R.

beats.scene: A woman holds an empty jewel case beside bare settings on a table
beats.summary: In broad daylight Lady Jerland's finest stones are stolen; Rozaine is arrested, then freed, and offers ten thousand francs for the thief.

beats.scene: A bound man lies in a dark corner of a ship's deck
beats.summary: The captain's watch vanishes and turns up in an officer's collar box; then Rozaine is found tied up and robbed, with a card thanking him for his reward.

beats.scene: A small old man with an umbrella waits at the foot of a gangway
beats.summary: At New York the detective Ganimard lets Rozaine pass, then stops Bernard d'Andrézy and says he is Arsène Lupin.

beats.scene: A young woman lets a small camera fall into the water beside a ship
beats.summary: Lupin had hidden the stolen money and jewels in a camera and given it to Nelly; she drops it into the water, and he sighs that he is not an honest man.

beats.scene: A baron reads a letter on a bridge before a castle
beats.summary: In Arsène Lupin in Prison, Baron Cahorn, alone in the castle of Malaquis with his treasures, gets a letter from Lupin in prison saying he will take them on the twenty-seventh of September.

beats.scene: A fat baron speaks to a small man fishing on a river bank
beats.summary: The baron reads that the detective Ganimard is fishing nearby, asks him for help, is refused, but after a new telegram from Lupin he pays three thousand francs for his protection.

beats.scene: Two big men sleep on chairs in a gallery with bare walls
beats.summary: On the night, the detective and two helpers guard the castle; at dawn the pictures, tapestries and jewels are gone, and the two assistants are drugged.

beats.scene: A gentleman in a bare prison cell greets a small visitor with a smile
beats.summary: The real Ganimard visits Lupin in his cell to ask about the Cahorn robbery; Lupin welcomes him like an old friend and admits it was all his work.

beats.scene: A prisoner smiles as he explains a plan to a puzzled detective
beats.summary: Lupin explains that the warning letter was bait, that a friend posed as the famous detective, and that two men lowered the treasures into a launch while the baron was kept busy.

beats.scene: A detective cracks an egg and finds a small blue paper inside
beats.summary: Lupin says the baron has already paid to get his goods back and shows a telegram hidden in an egg; he says he will not attend his own trial and returns Ganimard's watch.

beats.scene: Two inspectors search a bare prison cell while the prisoner is outside
beats.summary: In The Escape of Arsène Lupin, inspectors find a secret letter in a hollowed cigar and another in a hollow knife, about an automobile waiting for the prisoner.

beats.scene: A prisoner jumps from a prison van in a busy street among carriages
beats.summary: Alone in a prison van, Lupin escapes through a trapdoor when the van is stopped by a fallen horse, sits at a café, then walks back to the prison and asks to be let in.

beats.scene: A thin, stooping prisoner with a rough beard stands before a judge
beats.summary: Lupin has promised that he will not attend his trial; on the day a thin, dull man in the dock gives his name as Baudru Désiré and says nothing more.

beats.scene: A famous detective peers closely at a prisoner in a crowded court
beats.summary: Ganimard swears that the prisoner is not Lupin; the records show that Baudru was jailed by mistake two months earlier and the real Lupin has vanished.

beats.scene: A man laughs on a park bench as a detective seizes him
beats.summary: Baudru is freed and followed by Ganimard, who loses his assistants; in the Bois de Boulogne he bursts out laughing, and Ganimard knows the laugh of Lupin.

beats.scene: Two men talk in a quiet park, one laughing and one shaken
beats.summary: Lupin explains how diet, chemicals and practice slowly turned him into Baudru, how the van was a bluff, and leaves to dine with the British Ambassador.

beats.scene: A nervous lady and a smartly dressed stranger sit in a train compartment
beats.summary: In The Mysterious Traveller, a gentleman called Guillaume Berlat shares a train carriage with a nervous lady; a stranger jumps in at the last moment, and she whispers that Lupin is on the train.

beats.scene: A man kneels on another's chest in a train and ties his wrists
beats.summary: Berlat falls asleep; the stranger seizes, binds and robs him and takes the lady's jewels; Berlat is really Arsène Lupin himself.

beats.scene: A lady waves to policemen on a station platform beside a tied-up man
beats.summary: The thief leaps from the train in a tunnel; at Rouen Madame Renaud tells the commissary it was Lupin and vouches for Monsieur Berlat.

beats.scene: A fast automobile races beside an express train on a country road
beats.summary: Berlat tells the commissary that the thief will take a train from Darnétal and drives off with two policemen, winning a race with the express.

beats.scene: A man in a gray overcoat lies stunned outside a ruined hut
beats.summary: Berlat enters the wood alone, overpowers the thief in a hut, recovers his wallet, learns that he is the wanted criminal Pierre Onfrey, and leaves him for the police.

beats.scene: A countess in a ball gown wears a glittering historic necklace
beats.summary: In The Queen's Necklace, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise wears a famous necklace to a royal ball and her husband hides it that night; in the morning it is gone from a bolted, shut-in cabinet.

beats.scene: A police commissary examines a narrow window above a small courtyard
beats.summary: The police find the bolt and window untouched; suspicion falls on Henriette, a poor friend living in the house with her small son Raoul, but there is no proof.

beats.scene: A poor woman reads a letter that holds banknotes by candlelight
beats.summary: The countess dismisses Henriette; later Henriette receives two thousand francs every year from an unknown sender, until she dies six years afterwards.

beats.scene: A dinner party listens as a handsome guest explains an old theft
beats.summary: Years later at a dinner the Chevalier Floriani explains that the thief crossed from the kitchen window and opened a small upper window with a hooked poker; the count finds the hole.

beats.scene: A guest bows to a proud countess at the end of a dinner
beats.summary: The chevalier says only a child could pass the opening, Henriette's son; everyone understands that he is that son, who sold the diamonds one by one to help his mother.

beats.scene: A red leather case with a cardinal's arms lies open on a table
beats.summary: The countess answers that the necklace still belongs to her family; four days later the mounting is returned, and the newspapers say Lupin returned it.

beats.scene: A man lies rigid in bed watching a curtain move in a dark room
beats.summary: In The Seven of Hearts, a journalist finds a note ordering him not to move; all night he hears noises, and in the morning only a pierced playing card has appeared.

beats.scene: A stranger asks to be left alone in a library with mosaic walls
beats.summary: A man who read the journalist's article asks to stay alone in the library for three minutes; a shot is heard and he is found dead with a second seven of hearts and a banker's card.

beats.scene: A veiled lady speaks with two men after a startling newspaper article
beats.summary: A newspaper says the Varin brothers sold the plans of the submarine Seven-of-Hearts made by the vanished engineer Lacombe; Madame Andermatt, afraid of her letters, is advised to write to Salvator.

beats.scene: Two men dig in a vacant lot and find an iron plate
beats.summary: Daspry searches the house for the letters' hiding place; in a vacant lot they find old bones and an iron plate shaped like the seven of hearts; Salvator writes asking for the house that evening.

beats.scene: A man in a dim library presses an iron plate against a mosaic king
beats.summary: Hidden behind a curtain, they watch Varin and the banker quarrel; Daspry steps out, opens a safe in the mosaic king with the iron plate, takes the papers, returns the letters, and says that he is Arsène Lupin.

beats.scene: A man in a dark street rescues a gentleman from an attacker at night
beats.summary: In Madame Imbert's Safe, a young Lupin arranges an attack on the rich Ludovic Imbert, rescues him, gives the name Arsène Lupin and is invited to breakfast.

beats.scene: A young man lies on the floor looking through a pipe
beats.summary: The Imberts make Lupin their secretary and give him a room above the office; through a lead pipe in the floor he watches the safe, but cannot learn its combination.

beats.scene: A man slides down a rope outside a lit office window
beats.summary: When newspapers accuse the Imberts of fraud they count their bonds at midnight; Lupin descends a rope, overpowers Imbert gently, empties the safe, and next morning the Imberts have vanished.

beats.scene: An angry, laughing man waves his arms and tells a story to a friend
beats.summary: Later Lupin admits that the bonds were forgeries and that he had been used to pose as the invisible Brawford; Madame Imbert even owed him fifteen hundred francs.

beats.scene: A thief with a lantern kneels beside a still figure in a dark bedroom
beats.summary: In The Black Pearl, Lupin enters the Countess d'Andillot's apartment at night to take her black pearl; he finds the countess dead and the pearl gone from its box.

beats.scene: A servant in livery sits pale in a courtroom as a lawyer speaks
beats.summary: The servant Victor Danègre is arrested because of a lost button and blood spots, but at his trial his lawyer shows the gaps in the case and he is acquitted after six months.

beats.scene: Two men sit at a restaurant table, one pale and afraid, one calm
beats.summary: Under a false name Danègre is approached by the ex-inspector Grimaudan, who says the heiress sent him to recover the pearl and calls him the murderer.

beats.scene: A man lays a rusted knife and a copied key on a table
beats.summary: Grimaudan shows the copied key and the knife and describes a thumb mark in blood; he threatens to send a letter to the prosecutor, and Danègre gives in.

beats.scene: A man digs a black pearl from between wet paving stones at night
beats.summary: Danègre leads him to the street and shows where the pearl is hidden between two paving stones; Lupin pays for a ticket to America, and next day the newspapers say Lupin has the pearl.

beats.scene: Dinner guests laugh at a painter who looks like a famous thief
beats.summary: In Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late, the banker Devanne jokes that his guest Velmont looks like Lupin and announces that Sherlock Holmes will come to find the castle's secret passage.

beats.scene: Men carry furniture through a hidden door in a stone hall
beats.summary: Velmont says Devanne has given him the missing key; that night a bookcase turns and Lupin and eight men empty the Hall of the Guards through the secret passage.

beats.scene: A young lady with a candle faces a surprised thief in a dim gallery
beats.summary: Filling a bag with jewels in the gallery, Lupin is found by Miss Nelly, whom he knew from the ship; he drops everything and promises to return it all at three o'clock tomorrow.

beats.scene: Officers search a castle while guests at lunch glance at a clock
beats.summary: Police find no clue, though the stolen book is back on its shelf; Velmont arrives for lunch and Nelly keeps watching the clock for three o'clock.

beats.scene: Two army wagons roll into a castle courtyard as a girl watches
beats.summary: At three o'clock army wagons arrive with all the furniture under a forged order; Nelly points to a ruby ring on Lupin's finger; he leaves, and she leaves a white rose.

beats.scene: Two men meet on a narrow lane between high banks as horsemen pass
beats.summary: Lupin meets Sherlock Holmes in a lane and sends him to the castle; Holmes learns the goods are back and solves the secret passage by turning the third, fourth and eleventh letters.

beats.scene: A detective stands in a ruined chapel beside a stone tomb
beats.summary: The passage ends in a chapel with the tomb of Duke Rollo; a car sent by Velmont waits there with a package holding Holmes's watch, and Holmes vows that they will meet again.

B1B2: In The Arrest of Arsène Lupin, a wireless message reaches the liner La Provence in a storm. It says that the famous thief Arsène Lupin is on board, travelling alone, with fair hair and a wound on his right arm.

Miss Nelly Underdown and the Frenchman Bernard d'Andrézy study the passenger list for men travelling alone whose names begin with R. Only the fair-haired Monsieur Rozaine fits, and he says calmly that, by that reasoning, he ought to be arrested.

In broad daylight, someone steals the finest stones from Lady Jerland's jewels, leaving the empty settings on the table. The captain arrests Rozaine, but he is soon freed, and he offers ten thousand francs to anyone who finds the thief.

The captain's watch disappears and turns up in the second officer's collar box, as a joke. Then Rozaine is found tied up on deck, robbed of twenty thousand francs, with a card pinned to him signed Arsène Lupin.
At New York, the little detective Ganimard stands with his umbrella at the foot of the gangway and lets Rozaine pass. Then he stops Bernard d'Andrézy and says that he is Arsène Lupin.

Before his arrest, Lupin had put the stolen money and jewels into a camera and placed it in Nelly's hands. As she walks down the gangway, she lets it fall into the water, and Lupin sighs that he is not an honest man.

In Arsène Lupin in Prison, Baron Cahorn lives alone in a castle in the Seine, guarding his famous paintings. A letter from Lupin, who is in prison, says that he will take certain treasures on the night of the twenty-seventh of September.

The baron reads in a newspaper that the detective Ganimard is fishing at Caudebec, and he asks the little fisherman for help. The man refuses at first, but after a new telegram from Lupin, he agrees to guard the castle for three thousand francs.

On the night, the detective locks his two assistants in the gallery and waits with the baron in a small room. At dawn they find the gallery stripped of pictures and furniture, and the two men fast asleep, drugged.

The police chief sends the real Ganimard to ask Lupin in his cell about the robbery. Lupin welcomes him like an old friend, offers him a hard stool, and admits that the whole Cahorn affair was his work.

Lupin explains that his warning letter was the bait that made the baron ask for help. A friend of his, pretending to be the great Ganimard, kept the baron busy while two of his men carried away the treasures.

Lupin says the baron has already paid to get his goods back, and he shows a telegram hidden inside an egg. Then he announces that he will not be present at his trial, and he gives Ganimard back the watch he has taken.

In The Escape of Arsène Lupin, inspectors search Lupin's cell and find a secret letter hidden in a cigar. Another note, hidden inside a knife, speaks of an automobile that will wait for him every day.

Alone in a prison van, Lupin opens a hidden plate with his foot and jumps to the street when the traffic stops. After a drink at a café, he walks calmly back to the prison and asks the guard to let him in.

Lupin has promised that he will not be present at his trial, and the day arrives with the whole city waiting. But the thin, dull man in the dock gives the name Baudru Désiré and answers no other question.

Ganimard looks closely at the prisoner and swears on oath that he is not Arsène Lupin. A search of the records shows that a man named Baudru was jailed by mistake two months earlier, and Lupin has vanished.

After his release, the poor Baudru is followed by Ganimard, who loses his two assistants in the city. In the Bois de Boulogne, Baudru suddenly bursts out laughing, and Ganimard recognises the laugh of Lupin.

Lupin explains that he slowly changed his face and walk until he looked like the poor Baudru, whose place he took. Then he says goodbye to Ganimard, because he is dining that evening with the British Ambassador.

In The Mysterious Traveller, a gentleman called Guillaume Berlat takes a train to Rouen and shares a carriage with a lady. At the last moment, a well-dressed stranger jumps in, and the frightened lady whispers that Arsène Lupin is on the train.

Berlat falls asleep, and the stranger seizes him by the throat, ties his wrists and takes his wallet and the lady's jewels. Berlat is really Arsène Lupin, and he is annoyed to be robbed and bound like a beginner.

Passing through a tunnel, the thief puts on Berlat's overcoat and jumps from the slowing train. At Rouen, the lady tells the commissary that he is Arsène Lupin, and she says that Monsieur Berlat is a friend of her husband.

Berlat tells the commissary where the thief will catch a train, and he drives off with two policemen in his fast car. They beat the express to the next station, but the man jumps out and runs into a wood.
Berlat sends the two policemen to watch the edges of the wood and enters it alone. He finds the thief in a hut, takes back his wallet, and learns that the man is Pierre Onfrey, a wanted criminal.

In The Queen's Necklace, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise wears a famous necklace to a ball, and her husband hides it in a small cabinet. In the morning it has disappeared, although the door was bolted and the window was fastened.

The police examine the bolt and the window of the cabinet, but they find nothing. They suspect Henriette, a poor friend of the countess who lives in the house with her small son Raoul, but there is no proof.

The countess, still angry at her loss, dismisses poor Henriette from the house. Months later, Henriette begins to receive two thousand francs every year from an unknown sender, until she dies six years later.

Years later, at a dinner, the guests discuss the theft, and the polite Chevalier Floriani gives his opinion. He says the thief used a hooked poker through a hole in the window, and the count rushes out and finds the hole.

The chevalier says that only a small child could have crept through the opening, and that the child was Henriette's son. Everyone understands that he himself is that child, who sold the diamonds one by one to help his poor mother.

The proud countess tells the chevalier that the necklace still belongs to her family, even without its stones. Four days later she finds the old mounting on her table, and the newspapers say that Arsène Lupin returned it.

In The Seven of Hearts, a young journalist finds a note in his book that says he must not move or cry out. All night he hears loud noises, but in the morning nothing is missing, and he finds only a playing card with seven small holes.

A visitor who read the journalist's newspaper article asks to stay alone in the library for three minutes. A shot is heard, and he is found dead, with a second seven of hearts and a banker's card in his hand.

A newspaper writer called Salvator says that the Varin brothers sold the plans of a submarine, the Seven-of-Hearts, made by an engineer who vanished. Madame Andermatt, the banker's wife, then visits the journalist and his friend Jean Daspry, afraid because of some old letters.

Daspry searches the whole house for a hiding place, and then he and the journalist dig in a vacant lot. They find an old skeleton and a small iron plate in the form of a playing card with seven holes.

While Alfred Varin and the banker quarrel, Daspry steps out and uses the iron plate to open a safe hidden in a mosaic king. He takes the plans from Varin, gives letters to the banker, and tells Varin that his name is Arsène Lupin.

In Madame Imbert's Safe, a young man saves Ludovic Imbert from an attacker at night and gives his name, Arsène Lupin. The attack was arranged by Lupin himself, who wants to be invited into the rich Imbert house.

The Imberts are so grateful that they make Lupin their secretary and give him a room above Monsieur Imbert's office. Through a small pipe in the floor, he watches the great safe, but he cannot learn its combination.

When newspapers accuse them of fraud, the Imberts count their bonds at midnight, and Lupin climbs down a rope to their window. He ties up Monsieur Imbert without hurting him and empties the safe, and in the morning the Imberts have vanished.

Later, Lupin tells a friend that the stolen bonds were worthless forgeries, and that he had been played for a fool. The Imberts had used him as the mysterious Brawford to borrow money, and Madame Imbert still owed him fifteen hundred francs.
In The Black Pearl, Arsène Lupin enters an apartment at night to steal a famous black pearl. In the bedroom he finds the Countess d'Andillot lying dead, and the pearl is gone from its box.

The police arrest the countess's servant, Victor Danègre, because of a lost button and spots of blood on his waistcoat. His lawyer argues that the proof is weak, and after six months the jury sets him free.

Under a false name, the freed Danègre lives in fear until a stranger sits at his table in a restaurant. The man says he is ex-inspector Grimaudan, sent by the countess's heiress to recover the black pearl, and he calls Danègre the murderer.

Grimaudan holds up the duplicate key and the knife that Danègre had bought, and he describes a thumb mark that the police never found. He says that he will post a letter to the prosecutor unless the pearl is handed over that night.

Danègre leads Grimaudan to the street near the house, where the pearl lies hidden between two paving stones. Grimaudan pays him for a ticket to America, and next day the newspapers say that Arsène Lupin has the black pearl.

In Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late, the banker Devanne jokes that his guest, the painter Horace Velmont, looks like Arsène Lupin. He tells his guests that Sherlock Holmes is coming the next day to find a secret passage into his castle.

Velmont says that Devanne has just given him the missing key, and that he will rob the castle that night. At three in the morning, a bookcase turns, and Lupin and eight men carry the treasures away through a secret tunnel.

In a gallery, Lupin is filling a bag with watches and rings when a young woman comes down with a candle. It is Miss Nelly, from the ship, and he drops the treasure and promises to return everything at three o'clock tomorrow.

In the morning, officers search the castle and find no clue, except that the stolen book has been returned to the library. Velmont arrives at lunch as if nothing has happened, and Nelly keeps looking at the clock.

At three o'clock exactly, two army wagons arrive with all the stolen furniture, sent by a forged order. Lupin asks Nelly if he has kept his promise, and she only points to a ruby ring that he is wearing, so he leaves.

On the road to the station, Lupin politely meets Sherlock Holmes and shows him the way to the castle. At the castle, Holmes learns that the goods are back, and he finds the secret passage in ten minutes.

The secret passage ends in a ruined chapel, where Devanne's car is waiting because Velmont has sent it. In the car, a package from Lupin holds Holmes's own watch, and at the station Holmes vows that they will meet again.
C1C2: In the middle of a violent storm on the second day of the voyage, the wireless brought a message to the liner La Provence, and so begins the story called The Arrest of Arsène Lupin. It announced that the famous gentleman-burglar was travelling alone in the first class, with fair hair, a wound on his right forearm and a name beginning with R, but a flash of lightning cut off the rest. Within hours every passenger knew that the man whom the newspapers loved and the police hated, a master of disguises who robbed only castles and fine houses, was somewhere among them.

Miss Nelly Underdown, a rich and lovely girl who was travelling to see her father in Chicago, asked her admirer, the Frenchman Bernard d'Andrézy, whether he could find the thief by reason alone. He took out the passenger list and, by crossing off every man who was not alone, not fair-haired or not named with an R, he reduced thirteen names to one, Monsieur Rozaine. Rozaine, a pale and quiet young man who also admired Nelly, answered that he had reached the same conclusion and supposed that he ought to be arrested.

Lady Jerland ran from her cabin in despair, for while she was at tea a thief had forced the door and taken the finest stones from her jewels, leaving the empty settings on the table. The captain placed Rozaine under arrest that evening, but the next morning he was free again, since his papers were in order and his arms showed no wound. Humiliated, he offered a reward of ten thousand francs for the discovery of Lupin, and promised that if nobody helped him, he would unmask the thief himself.

The thief seemed to laugh at everyone, for the captain's watch vanished and was found next day in the collar box of the second officer. Then, one night, the officer on watch heard groans from a dark corner of the ship and found Rozaine lying there with his head wrapped in a scarf and his hands tied with a cord. A card pinned to his coat read that Arsène Lupin accepted with pleasure the ten thousand francs offered by Monsieur Rozaine, and in fact his stolen wallet had held twenty thousand.

When the liner reached America, the passengers streamed down the gangway under the eyes of an old man with an umbrella, who was none other than Ganimard, the detective who had sworn to catch Lupin. Poor Rozaine passed by without a glance, but Ganimard barred the way of Nelly and her escort and said quietly that the Frenchman was Arsène Lupin. When Bernard d'Andrézy protested that he was only himself, the detective replied that d'Andrézy had died in Macedonia three years earlier and struck him sharply on the right arm, where the wound had not healed.

Lupin, in the grip of Ganimard and his assistants, cared only about what Nelly would do with the camera in her hands, for the stolen banknotes and Lady Jerland's jewels lay hidden in it. She passed in front of him, glanced at the camera, and, as she went down the gangway, she let it fall with an air of clumsiness into the water between the ship and the quay. Lupin, who had lost the proof against him but also the girl, murmured to the astonished Ganimard, “What a pity that I am not an honest man.”

The old castle of Malaquis stands on a rock in the Seine, and there Baron Nathan Cahorn lived alone with three old servants, guarding three Rubens, two Watteaus and a fortune in furniture. One September day a postman brought him a registered letter from the Santé prison, signed Arsène Lupin, which described his best treasures with alarming accuracy and ordered him to send them to a Paris station within eight days. Otherwise, the writer warned politely, he would come and collect them himself on the night of the twenty-seventh, and the baron, though told that Lupin was safely locked up, could not stop trembling.

The baron read in a local newspaper that the great detective Ganimard was spending a holiday at Caudebec, and he found the little man fishing on the quay. The fisherman answered with pity that thieves do not warn their victims and that, in any case, Lupin was safely under lock and key, so the baron should go home and sleep. On the twenty-sixth of September, however, a telegram from Lupin arrived, telling him to prepare everything for the next night, and in his terror he returned and offered three thousand francs, which the fisherman accepted.

On the night of the twenty-seventh, the detective locked his two powerful assistants in the central gallery and carried away the keys, while he and the baron kept watch from a small room in the thick wall. Nothing happened except the sound of a distant automobile horn, and at daybreak the baron mounted the stairs radiant with joy, only to see that the walls were bare. The Rubens, the Watteaus and the tapestries had vanished, the doors and windows were intact, and the two assistants, who had drunk water from a carafe, lay in a heavy sleep from which nobody could wake them.

The police searched the castle for secret tunnels in vain, so Ganimard, the real one, who had grown friendly with Lupin on the voyage from America, asked leave to visit him in his cell. Lupin, lying on his bed, greeted him with a cry of joy, regretted that he could offer only a hard stool and no beer, and called him almost as clever as Sherlock Holmes. When Ganimard mentioned the Cahorn affair, the prisoner admitted cheerfully that he had managed it from beginning to end, and he even took from the drawer of a plain wooden table the receipts for his letter and telegram.

Since a castle cannot be entered by force, said Lupin, the owner must be made to invite the thief, and so he had written the baron a warning letter that no policeman would take seriously. Then a friend of his had made a newspaper announce that the famous Ganimard was fishing nearby, so that the frightened baron would run to him for help and pay him well. While the false detective kept the baron company, two members of the gang drugged the guards and lowered the pictures by rope into a launch on the river.

Lupin declared that the affair was already settled, since the baron had paid a hundred thousand francs for the return of his treasures through the false detective. He told Ganimard to break the egg on his lunch tray, and inside the shell lay a small blue telegram announcing that the contract was closed. Then, promising that he would not be present at his own trial, he returned the watch that had strayed from the detective's pocket into his own.

While Lupin was out for exercise, Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant searched his cell in the Santé and found nothing until a guard pointed to the drawer, where lay a fine cigar with a gold band. The chief of the Sûreté, Monsieur Dudouis, squeezed it, discovered a thin roll of paper inside, and read a woman's message about a basket, eight compartments and an automobile that would wait every day from twelve to four. That evening a second note, hidden in the hollow handle of the prisoner's knife, told him to trust his friend, and the police rejoiced, since they could now trap not only Lupin but his whole gang.

One afternoon Lupin was alone in the prison van, and as it crept through the traffic of Paris he pressed his foot on a metal plate that moved, and when the van stopped he dropped to the street and ran. He sat down at a café, ordered a beer, and told the amazed proprietor that he had forgotten his purse but that the name Arsène Lupin, escaped prisoner, should be enough to give him credit. Then, strolling on to the Santé, he told the sentinel that he wished to return to his cell, and he explained to the keeper that the attempt was only a trap and that he would escape when he chose.

Lupin had promised the whole of Paris that he would not be present at his own trial, and on a dark, rainy morning the court was full of people hoping to see a great prank. The prisoner who was led in, however, was thin and stooped, with an earth-coloured face, a straggling beard and a vacant stare, and when the judge asked his name, he muttered in a thick voice that it was Baudru, Désiré. The judge, who took this for yet another alias or an attempt to pass for an idiot, read out the long list of Lupin's crimes, but the man only shuffled his feet and grunted.

When the nervous detective Ganimard was called to give evidence, he stopped, looked sharply at the prisoner, and asked leave to examine him closely, and after several minutes he declared on his oath that this was not Arsène Lupin. The judge was thunderstruck, but the gaolers admitted that for two months the man in cell twenty-four had lain with his face to the wall, and he himself said he had been arrested by mistake. The records proved that a poor man called Baudru Désiré had left the Dépôt on the very day when Lupin left it in a van, and the court understood that the real Lupin had long since vanished.

Because the court could not keep an innocent man in prison, Baudru Désiré was set free on a foggy January morning, and Ganimard and two inspectors followed him through Paris in the hope that he would lead them to Lupin. At a busy omnibus station the shabby man slipped out by a second exit and left the assistants behind, but Ganimard saw him and followed alone to a bench beside a pond in the Bois de Boulogne. When he sat down beside him and made some remark about the weather, the man burst into a happy, spontaneous laugh, and Ganimard felt his hair stand on end, for it was the laugh of Arsène Lupin.

Lupin explained, with an air of modesty, that a dozen years of study had taught him to change his appearance at will, and that in his cell he had spent two months dieting and practising grimaces. The guards never noticed the slow change, and the real Baudru, a harmless beggar who resembled him slightly, had spent a night at the Dépôt, so that the police would believe in a substitution. The van and the letters, he said, were only a trick to make the public expect his escape, and he left Ganimard to dress for a dinner with the British Ambassador.

A gentleman known to his friends as Guillaume Berlat took the train from Paris to Rouen and chose a compartment where a young lady sat alone, whose husband kissed her goodbye on the platform. Just as the whistle sounded, a man burst in, elegantly dressed and with an intelligent face that Berlat felt he had seen before, and the lady turned pale and drew her little travelling bag closer to her. When Berlat asked if she was ill, she whispered that Arsène Lupin was on the train, though she gazed all the time at the stranger and not at him.

Berlat, overcome by tiredness, fell asleep in spite of the lady's warnings, and he woke to find the stranger kneeling on his chest and gripping his throat, and a moment later he was bound and gagged like a mummy. The thief calmly took his purse and wallet, and then the lady's jewels, which she handed over with a swoon, and then he lit a cigarette and admired his booty. The man who had been robbed was Arsène Lupin himself, who felt both the humour and the danger of the situation, since the police at Rouen might soon find him tied up and ready to be delivered.

In a tunnel, the thief put on Berlat's overcoat, took the lady's umbrella, opened the door when the train slowed down, and leaped to the ground, so that the lady revived at once and lamented her lost jewels. Berlat, whose gag she removed, told her to say that his name was Guillaume Berlat, a friend of her husband, and to describe the thief in a soft hat and a gray overcoat. At Rouen she cried out to the commissary of police that Arsène Lupin had attacked them, and the man in charge, who had not the slightest suspicion of his fellow traveller, took her story as truth.

Berlat explained to the delighted commissary that the thief must be going from Darnétal to Amiens, and he offered his own fast automobile and two policemen, Massol and Delivet, for the pursuit. They arrived at Darnétal a few minutes too late, but they raced the express along the road, winning by twenty lengths, and reached the next station before it. The thief, who must have seen them, leaped from the train and ran into a thick grove, and the swiftest policeman followed until Berlat told him to wait.

Berlat posted Massol and Delivet on two sides of the grove and entered alone, so that no officer would see the papers in his wallet, and he soon found his man hiding in a ruined hut on a mound. He threw him to the ground, and when the thief tried to stab him, he stunned him with a blow, recovered his wallet, and found on an envelope the name of Pierre Onfrey, a wanted criminal. He left two banknotes and a card of thanks for the policemen, kept the lady's jewels, fired a shot in the air to call them, and next day the newspapers gave Lupin the credit for the arrest.

Two or three times each year the Countess de Dreux-Soubise wore on her white shoulders the historic jewel called The Queen's Necklace, which her family had kept for nearly a century. One evening, at a royal reception, she achieved a great triumph, and when they came home her husband put the necklace in its red leather case on a high shelf in a small cabinet beyond their bed. Next morning, although the bedroom door had been bolted all night, the count entered the cabinet and found that the shelf was empty.

The commissary of police found the bolt intact and the cabinet window fastened, and the examining judge, who explored the little inner court from top to bottom, found nothing either. All inquiries turned toward Henriette, a school friend of the countess who had married beneath her, who lived with her six-year-old son Raoul in a poor room at the end of the corridor and sewed for the countess. Yet the judge could prove nothing against her, for she had left the house only four times in three years, and after four months he closed the inquiry, believing that the count and countess had secretly sold the necklace.

The Dreux-Soubise, deprived of the credit that such a treasure gave them, lived in some difficulty, and the countess, wounded in her pride, treated her old school friend more and more severely until Henriette was dismissed. Some months afterwards Henriette received a letter, posted in Paris, with two banknotes of one thousand francs each and no name, and she wrote to the countess to thank her, thinking that she was the sender. A similar letter reached her every year for six years, the last two containing double the sum, and when she died the mystery of the unknown benefactor remained unsolved.

Years later the count and countess gave a dinner, and when the guests spoke of the Queen's Necklace, the Chevalier Floriani, a man from Sicily whom the count had met at Palermo, said that the problem was simple. Since a bolted door cannot be opened from outside, he said, the thief must have crossed from the kitchen window by a bridge of boards and opened the little upper window with a hooked poker. The count laughed at this, but at the chevalier's insistence he left the room, and returned pale and trembling to say that a hole made for the poker was exactly where he had said.

Since no man could crawl through so small an opening, said the chevalier, the thief must have been Henriette's son, who had used the kitchen shelves as a bridge and hidden the necklace among his school books. The count, returning from the kitchen, confirmed that the shelves had been unnailed, and the chevalier went on to describe how the boy had sold a diamond each year and sent the money to his mother. His voice shook with feeling as he spoke, and every guest understood that Floriani was Henriette's son, who had come to face the family that had wronged her.

The countess, trembling with humiliated pride, answered that the necklace was the pride of her house and belonged to the Dreux-Soubise as much as their name, even though its stones had been sold. She asked him to tell the thief to give it back, and four days later she found on her table a red leather case stamped with the cardinal's arms, in which lay the famous mounting. The next day the newspapers announced that Arsène Lupin had recovered the Queen's Necklace and hastened to return it, so that the boy who had once crept through the little window was plainly Lupin himself.

On the night of the twenty-second of June, the young journalist who tells this story came home to his lonely house at Neuilly and found, in the book beside his bed, a sealed note. The note said that, whatever happened, he must not move or utter a cry, and all night he lay frozen with fear, listening to hammering in his library and watching a curtain. At dawn he fired at the curtain and found nobody there and nothing missing, but under a rug lay a playing card, the seven of hearts, each red spot pierced by a round hole.

A few days after the journalist's story appeared in the newspaper, a rough-looking man of forty called on him and asked to be left alone in the library for three minutes, since the details agreed with another case he knew. After two and three-quarter minutes the journalist heard a pistol shot, ran upstairs, and found the man lying dead on the floor with a revolver near his hand. Two feet away lay a second seven of hearts, and in the dead man's hand was a card bearing the name of Georges Andermatt, a rich banker, who identified the man as Etienne Varin but could not explain the card.

The newspaper article, signed Salvator, told how a young engineer named Louis Lacombe had vanished after dining with the banker Andermatt, ten years earlier. It added that the Varin brothers, who had worked with him, had sold the plans of his submarine, now built abroad under the name Seven-of-Hearts. Madame Andermatt then visited the journalist and his friend Jean Daspry, confessing that the Varins also held some letters of hers, and Daspry told her to write to Salvator, who was working against them, not against her husband.

Daspry, who suspected that the letters were hidden in the library, tapped every wall, floor and ceiling, and when he found nothing he led the journalist with a pickaxe and spade to the vacant lots nearby. In a corner, under a heap of earth and briars, the two men unearthed the bones of a man and an iron plate cut like a playing card, with seven red spots, each pierced by a hole. The journalist, who went to bed with a fever, received on the third day a polite letter from Salvator asking him to lend his house that evening for a meeting between two enemies.

Hidden behind a curtain, the journalist, Daspry and Madame Andermatt watched Alfred Varin and the banker quarrel until Varin drew a revolver and Daspry stepped out and shot it from his hand. Holding up the iron plate, Daspry applied it to the sword of the mosaic king and pressed seven stones with an awl, and a hidden safe opened, with a smaller one inside it that held the package of letters. He took Lacombe's papers from Varin, gave the banker only copies of the letters and the real ones to his wife, and told Varin that his name was Arsène Lupin.

At three o'clock one winter morning, Ludovic Imbert was attacked on the boulevard by a man who threw him down and gagged him, until a stranger arrived with a cane and put the attacker to flight. The rescued man took him home in a carriage and asked his name, and the stranger handed him a card that read Arsène Lupin, a name he had just invented. In truth the attacker was Lupin's own friend, for he had spent six months planning to enter the house of the Imberts, who were said to own a hundred millions in a safe.

Madame Imbert, a short, plump and talkative woman, treated Lupin as an old friend and soon made him private secretary to herself and her husband for a hundred francs a month, with a room directly above Monsieur Imbert's office. Lupin, who had little to do, drilled a small pipe through the floor and spent his days stretched on the boards, watching the couple at their immense safe of iron and steel. Strangely, the servants never knew his name and called him only monsieur, while the Imberts spoke of him as a barbarian who liked solitude, and he kept silent and waited for his chance.

When some newspapers accused the Imberts of swindling, they decided to make an inventory of the contents of the safe, and Lupin, guessing that it would be that night, locked himself in his room and waited. At midnight he slid down a knotted rope to the office balcony, where Monsieur Imbert was working alone, and when Imbert rose to close the window, Lupin stunned him and bound him without the slightest injury. In two trips, with a carriage waiting in the street, he emptied the safe, and next morning the newspapers announced that Ludovic and Gervaise Imbert had disappeared.

One day, pacing the room with a feverish eye, Lupin confessed to his friend the writer that the bonds he had stolen were not worth the paper they were printed on, for every one of them was a forgery. The Imberts' great fortune, he had learned from the newspapers, was a fiction, and the quiet eccentric whom the servants called monsieur had been shown to bankers as old André Brawford, whose supposed millions were the security for their loans. Worst of all, he said, with a burst of laughter at his own expense, Madame Imbert had also borrowed fifteen hundred francs from him for her poor and had never paid them back.

At three in the morning a late visitor rang for a doctor in the avenue Hoche, climbed to the fifth floor, opened an apartment door with a key, and arranged an escape by blocking the street door's lock. Arsène Lupin had a plan of the rooms, and he knew that the old singer, the Countess d'Andillot, hid in a box of writing paper the black pearl that an emperor had given her. In her bedroom, crawling in the dark, he touched cold hair, saw by his lantern that the countess lay dead, and found her box empty, so that instead of a quiet theft he faced a murder.

The newspapers described the murder of the famous singer Léotine Zalti, who had kept only the black pearl from all her jewels, and soon the police arrested her servant, Victor Danègre, a known drunkard. Blood spots were found on his waistcoat and a button from it lay under the victim's bed, but nobody could show how he had left the locked apartment, who had made the key, or where the knife was. At the trial his lawyer pointed out all these gaps, the jury returned a verdict of acquittal, and Danègre left prison after six months, weak, haunted by nightmares and in terror of being followed.

Living at Montmartre under the false name of Anatole Dufour, Danègre was eating in a restaurant one evening when a stranger sat at his table and drank to the health of Victor Danègre. The man handed him a card that read Grimaudan, former inspector of detectives, and said that he was acting for Mademoiselle de Sinclèves, the countess's heiress, who wanted the black pearl back. When Danègre swore that he had never stolen it, Grimaudan replied calmly that he was the murderer, and began to tell him how he knew.

Calmly, Grimaudan told Danègre that he had ordered a copy of the cook's key three weeks before the crime and had bought a knife with a grooved blade on the same day. He added that Danègre had left a thumb-mark in blood on the wall of the wardrobe closet, and then he laid the key and the rusted knife on the table, saying that the clerk and the locksmith would recognise him. Danègre, shaking with fear, asked what he would be paid for the pearl, and Grimaudan answered that he would get his life, for otherwise a letter from the heiress would go to the public prosecutor that night.

Defeated, Danègre walked beside Grimaudan to the street near the Parc Monceau, sat down on a bench, and said that the pearl lay buried in the gutter, between the twelfth and thirteenth paving stones. Grimaudan dug it out with his penknife and paid the murderer two hundred francs for a steerage ticket to America, and the next morning the newspapers announced that Arsène Lupin had recovered the black pearl. Lupin explained later that, in forty minutes in that room, he had decided to have a servant arrested, and so he had left the button, taken the knife and the key, and let the law do the rest.

At the Château de Thibermesnil, the banker Georges Devanne laughed at dinner that his guest, the painter Horace Velmont, looked so much like Arsène Lupin that he would have called the police if he had not known him. He then announced that the great Sherlock Holmes would arrive the next afternoon, because a rare book describing the castle's secret passage had been stolen, and the copy in the National Library had been taken too. Nobody knew where the passage ended in the great hall, said Devanne, since the only clues were an old riddle about a bee and an eye, and the numbers three, four, eleven written by King Louis the Sixteenth.

Velmont laughed and thanked Devanne for the one detail that had been missing, the key to the riddle, and added that he must rob the castle that very night, before Holmes came. Devanne drove him to Dieppe, fetched some friends from the midnight train, and went to bed, and at three o'clock in the morning a section of the bookcase turned on a pivot in the dark silence. Arsène Lupin and eight men then entered the hall and, in forty minutes, carried the chairs, tapestries, paintings and statuettes into the tunnel, until the room was bare.

In the glass cabinet of the gallery, Lupin found watches, snuff-boxes, rings and miniatures, and he was stuffing them into a linen bag and his pockets when he heard a step and hid behind a window curtain. A young woman with a candle came down the stairs, saw the broken cabinet, and drew aside the curtain, and the two faced each other in astonishment. She was Miss Nelly Underdown, who had once dropped his camera into the sea, and Lupin, ashamed to be seen as a common thief, emptied his pockets and promised that everything would be returned the next day at three o'clock.

Devanne spent the morning among gendarmes and officers, who found no footprint, no broken lock, and no clue of how the thieves had entered. The only strange thing was that the stolen book of the National Library lay on the shelf next to its twin, although Devanne thought it absurd to suspect the famous painter. At noon Velmont arrived, calm and smiling, and took Nelly in to lunch, though she, pale and silent, hardly heard a word he said, and on the terrace she kept her eyes on the great clock, remembering his promise.

As the clock struck three, two army wagons rolled into the courtyard, and a sergeant explained that, by an order signed by a colonel, he had collected the furniture from a crossroads in the forest. The officers declared the signature a clever forgery, the goods went back into their places, and Lupin approached Nelly at the end of the terrace and asked quietly whether he had not kept his promise. Without a word she pointed to the ruby ring on his finger, which belonged to Devanne, and he bowed and walked away, but found afterwards a white rose that she had left on a flower box.

On the road to the station, in a ravine between two steep banks, Lupin met a tall Englishman with a heavy cane, who asked the way to the castle. Lupin answered, with a touch of irony, that Sherlock Holmes had no warmer admirer than himself, and the two men studied each other like equal forces while the gendarmes rode past. Holmes then went on to the castle, learned that the goods were back, and in ten minutes solved the secret of the passage by turning the third, fourth and eleventh letters of the word Thibermesnil.

Following the tunnel with a lantern, Holmes and Devanne came out in the ruined chapel, where a block of granite swung aside to form the tomb of Duke Rollo. A motor car was waiting there, sent by Monsieur Velmont, who had known that the solution would be simple for the great detective, and in its pocket lay a small package marked Sherlock Holmes, from Arsène Lupin. It held Holmes's own watch, which Lupin had taken on the road, and the Englishman, silent and furious all the way to the station, said at last that he and Lupin would surely meet again.
